RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Vandals in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Silesia & Upper Danube, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Vandals was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Silesia & Upper Danube, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Mule carts groan through the Silesian ruts, and the rye issued to our company has gone grey and sour. Pay arrives as clipped copper, which must be spent in the nearest market town or it loses value. A spearman learns to count his coins twice before buying boots, and he prays the next raid on a merchant convoy will put real silver in his hands.

Two forges on the estate ran hot through the autumn, turning out one hundred and fifty horseshoes and sixty spearheads. The reeve sells cured hides and salt fish at the river fair, and the proceeds pay for the mail of the household knights. He keeps two sets of accounts, one for the house and one for the toll officers who inspect every wagon bound for the Danube markets.
